newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: "Security clause" at centre of EU-U.S. trade row.
newsitem.headline: "Security clause" at centre of EU-U.S. trade row.

text.p: Is the United States facing an immediate threat to its national security from Fidel Castro's Cuba?
That is the political question a panel of international experts appointed on Thursday by the World Trade Organisation (WTO) will have to consider.

Washington says the Cuban threat justifies approval last February by President Bill Clinton of the Helms-Burton law aimed at stopping foreign investment in the communist island's cash-strapped economy.
U.S. officials say the action is legal under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), the set of open trading rules which underpins the two-year-old WTO.
They point to the GATT's Article XXI, in existence since the Agreement was signed by the United States and a handful of other countries -- ironically in Havana -- in 1947, but never tested.

That article, "Security Exceptions", says nothing in the overall accord should be construed "to prevent any contracting party from taking any action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests."

Implication of the U.S. argument, contested by the European Union and other WTO members, is that this allows any country to declare unilaterally that its security is endangered and suspend its open trade obligations under the GATT.

However, the article also sets three areas under which its provisions can be applied -- in relation to "fissionable material", to traffic in arms, or to action "taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations."
Trade lawyers say Washington would he hard put to prove that Cuba's downing of two small planes flown by anti-Castro exiles off the island last January had created such an emergency.

But they also accept that there is justification in the U.S. argument that if the President of the United States deems his country faces a security threat, it would be disingenuous for an international trade panel to contradict him.
Article XXI was invoked three times during the 47-year history of the GATT -- when as well as a treaty it was also an organisation administering agreed trade rules.
In 1961, Ghana used the article to justify a boycott on Portuguese goods as part of a battle against colonialism.

In 1975 Sweden, arguing an uninterrupted supply of boots for its army could be threatened if it allowed cheaper foreign military footwear to swamp the market and undermine national producers, slapped a ban on imports.
And in 1978, the United States said its trade embargo on the left-wing Sandinista government of Nicaragua was covered by Article XXI.

Even Castro's Cuba, a founder member of the GATT under its pre-communist rulers, did not challenge the 35-year-old trade boycott imposed by Washington after the 1959 revolution, realising that under the old rules it could get nowhere.
For under the GATT, any country could indefinitely block any action in the body against it in a trade dispute by simply refusing consensus.

But under the WTO, and the tougher rules on which the United States itself insisted, such manouevring is no longer possible. Consensus can only be refused once, and if a panel finds a country is breaking the rules, the WTO can authorise others to apply sanctions against the violator.
"This certainly doesn't make the panel's job any easier," said one trade official. "But it certainly makes things very interesting. It's a whole new ball game."
